issues.legal_issue: The statutory doctrine of frustration exhaustively governs frustration of contracts in India.
material_facts: The lessee sought a refund on the ground that communal riots and the resulting inability to remain in the area made performance of the lease covenants impossible.
The court considered whether the doctrine of frustration could be enlarged by principles drawn from English common law.
issues.conclusion: Section 56 of the Contract Act exhaustively governs contractual frustration in India, and courts cannot supplement it with English common-law principles outside the statute.
issues.legal_principle: Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act governs discharge of contracts for supervening impossibility or illegality. As stated in Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur & Co., where the Indian Contract Act deals with a subject, it is exhaustive on that subject and English-law principles cannot be imported outside its provisions. The contrary view in Parshotam Das Shankar Das v. Municipal Committee, Batala was overruled to that extent.

predicates.contract_frustration_dispute: A party seeks to be discharged from contractual obligations because a later event allegedly made performance impossible or unlawful.
predicates.supervening_event_affects_performance: An event occurring after the agreement allegedly affects the ability to perform it.

issues.definition: When a dispute seeks discharge of contractual obligations because of a later event affecting performance, the statutory rule governing frustration is exhaustive.

issues.legal_issue: Frustration of a contract does not invalidate a completed transfer of property created by a lease.
material_facts: The parties had entered into a lease, the lessee had obtained possession, and the rights under the lease had vested.
The lessee relied on events arising after the lease to claim that the lease should no longer bind him.
There was no claim that the lease itself was void or voidable, or that it had been determined in a manner recognized by law.
issues.conclusion: Section 56 does not apply to invalidate a completed transfer created by a lease, although a lease covenant to perform an act may become void if that act later becomes impossible or unlawful.
issues.legal_principle: Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act applies to contracts and does not invalidate a completed transfer of property. Section 4 of the Transfer of Property Act does not incorporate the Contract Act into the Transfer of Property Act. The court distinguished an executory contract from a completed conveyance: events that discharge a contract do not invalidate a concluded transfer. A covenant under a lease may be affected by section 56, but that does not void the transfer resulting from the lease.

predicates.completed_lease_dispute: A dispute concerns rights created by a lease of immovable property that has been granted and acted upon.
predicates.lease_transfer_completed: The lease has transferred the right to enjoy the property to the lessee.
predicates.supervening_event_impairs_use: An event occurring after the lease makes the lessee's use of the property difficult or impossible.

issues.definition: If a dispute concerns a completed lease transfer and a later event impairs use of the property, frustration does not invalidate the completed lease.

issues.legal_issue: A lessee cannot avoid a lease merely because the lessee is unable to use the property when it has not been destroyed or rendered substantially and permanently unfit for its leased purpose.
material_facts: The leased agricultural land was not destroyed and had not become permanently unfit for agriculture.
The lessee had obtained possession, carried on agricultural operations, and partly enjoyed their benefit.
The lessee became unable to continue effective possession and cultivation because of widespread riots and migration.
The lease contained no agreement that rent would not be payable if the lessee could not personally supervise cultivation or collect the crops.
issues.conclusion: Because the land was neither destroyed nor rendered substantially and permanently unfit for agriculture, the lessee could not avoid the lease or recover rent merely because the riots prevented effective use of the land.
issues.legal_principle: Transfer of Property Act section 108(e) permits a lessee, at the lessee's option, to avoid a lease if a material part of the property is wholly destroyed or rendered substantially and permanently unfit for its leased purpose by fire, tempest, flood, violence of an army or mob, or other irresistible force. The principle applies to agricultural leases and to leases in areas where the Transfer of Property Act has not been extended. Mere inability to use the property does not suffice. The court referred to Abdul Hashem v. Balahari Mondal, Tarabai Jivanlal Parekh v. Lala Padamchand, Alanduraiappar Koil Chithakkadu v. T. S. A. Hamid, and Sri Amuruvi Perumal Devasthanam v. K. R. Sabapathi Pillai, and rejected the contrary observations in Gurdarshan Singh v. Bishen Singh on frustration applying to leases.

rule.if: lease_avoidance_dispute and lease_property_not_destroyed and lease_property_not_substantially_permanently_unfit and lessee_unable_to_use_land

predicates.lease_avoidance_dispute: A lessee seeks to avoid a lease because events have prevented use of the leased property.
predicates.lease_property_not_destroyed: The leased property has not been wholly destroyed.
predicates.lease_property_not_substantially_permane: The leased property has not become substantially and permanently unfit for the purpose for which it was leased.
predicates.lessee_unable_to_use_land: The lessee is unable to use the land for the leased purpose.

issues.definition: When a lessee seeks to avoid a lease because the land cannot be used, but the land is neither destroyed nor substantially and permanently unfit, the lessee cannot avoid the lease for nonuse.
